comparison: Both evaluations support the migration defect findings (C4-C6, C52-C57, C128-C143). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and sample sizes, while peer reviewers describe the analysis as 'extensive and convincing' with 'impressive approaches.' Both agree the data strongly support these claims about aberrant migration, nucleokinesis, and centrokinesis defects.

Both evaluations support the centrosome-related findings (C59-C60, C62, C144-C152). OpenEval validates the statistical methods and sample sizes, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm the FMRP-MAP1B axis affects centrosome and nucleus movement during saltatory migration. Complete agreement on these claims.

Perfect alignment on cell-autonomous nature of defects (C7, C36, C63-C65, C68). Both evaluations support the miRNA knockdown experiments showing 64% FMRP reduction and recapitulation of migratory defects. Peer reviewers explicitly state this 'nicely supports the idea that FMRP have a cell autonomous function.'

Both support MAP1B overexpression findings (C8, C40, C76, C84, C110, C112). OpenEval validates the 1.6× increase with statistical significance, while peer reviewers confirm MAP1B overexpression and state results 'strongly suggest that FMRP-MAP1B axis has an important role in regulation of the neuroblasts tangential migration.'

Both evaluations support the MAP1B knockdown rescue experiments (C9, C78-C81). OpenEval emphasizes statistical validation and adequate sample sizes, while peer reviewers describe the rescue as 'discreet and elaborate' that 'successfully' rescues most migratory defects. Strong agreement on rescue efficacy.

Both support the finding that sinuosity defects persist despite MAP1B knockdown (C82-C83). OpenEval interprets this as evidence for multiple molecular pathways, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this by acknowledging 'most' but not all defects are rescued. Agreement on the observation.

Perfect alignment on microtubular cage findings (C10-C11, C42-C43, C85-C88, C118-C119, C153-C156). Both evaluations support the new data showing FMRP-MAP1B axis affects microtubule cage organization. Peer reviewers explicitly state these results 'elaborate FMRP and MAP1B participation in microtubule organization' and 'reinforce' the association with defects.

Both evaluations support the main mechanistic conclusion (C44, C89-C90, C126) linking FMRP to MAP1B to microtubule organization to migration. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of multiple evidence lines, while peer reviewers describe it as 'valuable new information' that 'emphasizes the interplay between FMRP, MAP1B, and the microtubule cytoskeleton.'

Both evaluations rate these claims as UNCERTAIN (C66-C67). OpenEval notes the mechanistic explanation about environmental versus cell-autonomous contributions to directionality defects remains speculative without additional experiments. Peer reviewers do not explicitly address these nuanced interpretations, providing no validation for the speculative claims.

Divergent evaluations on functional consequences (C102-C103). OpenEval supports these claims based on prior citations (Bocchi et al. 2017), while Reviewer 3 explicitly raises concern that 'functional consequences of delay in neuroblast migration in the integration and function of OB interneurons and this relation with FXS pathophysiology' remain inadequately addressed, noting 'An anatomical examination of the RMS in the Fmr1KO mice is still missing.'

OpenEval supports background claims about FXS prevalence and autism association (C1-C2, C12-C13) as well-established facts. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focused on experimental findings rather than background literature.
